extraction.title: Competitive Influence Maximization in Social Networks
extraction.document_type: Theoretical computer science paper (conference-style; inferred from "full version due to space constraints" and the Proc. citations; the text does not state venue or year)
extraction.coverage: Full text read in one pass (text lines 1-336, all of 16802 chars), including abstract, introduction, model, best-response analysis, first-mover analysis, tree FPTAS, proofs, acknowledgments and references. Some proofs (Lemma 3, Lemma 4 is given; Lemma 3 deferred) and the directed-line and arborescence extensions are stated as deferred to a full version and are not in this text.
extraction.research_question: How do multiple players (companies or innovations) competing by viral word-of-mouth choose initial seed sets in a social network under a generalized independent cascade model? Specifically: best responses to an opponent's strategy, the efficiency of equilibria ("price of competition"), first-mover strategies in a two-player duopoly, and whether single-player influence maximization admits an FPTAS on bidirected trees.
extraction.theory: Independent cascade model of diffusion (Goldenberg et al.; Kempe, Kleinberg, Tardos), extended to multiple competing colors. Motivated by Hotelling's model of competition and by competitive facility location and Voronoi games (text lines 47-48). Uses submodular utility systems (Vetta) and submodular maximization via greedy (Nemhauser, Wolsey, Fisher).
extraction.data: None. Purely theoretical analysis; no sample, unit of analysis, time period, or N is reported.
extraction.method: Formal model definition with exponentially distributed activation delays and random color tie-breaking (Section 2, lines 63-85). Best-response analysis via a deterministic equivalent of the random process and proof of monotone submodularity of expected reach (Lemma 1, Section 3). Approximation via greedy for submodular maximization. Equilibrium efficiency via Vetta's utility-system theorem (Section 3). First-mover analysis on lines via dynamic programming over a cutoff point c, with Lemma 2 (optimal solution cuts each line into equal pieces) (Section 4). FPTAS for bidirected trees via dynamic programming over subtree values G(v,k,q+,q-) with probability rounding at granularity delta = epsilon/n^3 and an inductive error bound (Theorem 3, Section 5).
extraction.identification: Not applicable. No empirical identification strategy; results are worst-case approximation and proof-based guarantees.
extraction.scope: Population, institution, and era: none. Scope is abstract graphs: directed graphs G=(V,E) with edge activation probabilities; two-player duopoly for first-mover results (Section 4); multi-player game for best response and price of competition; bidirected trees for the FPTAS (with the extension to bounded treewidth claimed but not shown).

key_findings.finding: Best response to fixed opponent strategies: player i's expected reach is a monotone and submodular function of S_i, so greedy gives a (1-1/e) approximation to the best response for the last player to commit.
key_findings.location: Section 3, Lemma 1 and Theorem 1 (abstract lines 15-16; intro lines 51-52; proof lines 92-120)
key_findings.numbers: approximation factor (1 - 1/e)

key_findings.finding: Price of competition (uncoordinated equilibria vs. single controller with all seeds) is at most 2, via Vetta's utility-system theorem applied to the total activated set, which is monotone submodular in the union of seeds.
key_findings.numbers: factor 2

key_findings.finding: Game has no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium in general, but mixed-strategy Nash equilibria exist.

Two-player first-mover game on disjoint lines: the optimal solution cuts every line into equal-sized pieces, so the red player need only try n*k candidate cutoff values l_i/j (i=1..n, j=1..k), giving a strongly polynomial dynamic program.
key_findings.location: Section 4, Lemma 2 and paragraph at lines 149-153
key_findings.numbers: n*k candidate cutoff values; lines of lengths l_1..l_n; k cuts

key_findings.finding: FPTAS for single-player influence maximization on bidirected trees, including unequal probabilities in opposite edge directions: a 1-epsilon approximation, with rounding granularity delta = epsilon/n^3 and additive error at most delta*n^3 <= epsilon <= epsilon*OPT.
key_findings.location: Section 5, Theorem 3 and the closing paragraph after its proof (lines 176-231)
key_findings.numbers: delta = epsilon/n^3; approximation 1-epsilon; additive error <= epsilon*OPT

key_findings.finding: Conjecture (not proven): influence maximization is NP-complete even for arborescences directed into a root. The general problem is already known NP-complete (cited to [3,4]) and APX-hard (cited to [3]).

limitations: Several proofs are deferred to a full version because of space constraints: Lemma 3 proof, and the extensions of the first-mover line algorithm to directed lines and outdirected arborescences (lines 168-171, 299-300).
The arborescence NP-completeness result is only conjectured (lines 59-60).
The FPTAS extension to bounded-treewidth graphs is asserted with a significant increase in complexity but not shown (lines 177-178).

The game has no pure-strategy Nash equilibria in general (lines 83-85), so equilibrium results rely on mixed strategies, and the reasoning about the price of competition relies on Vetta's theorem as cited.
Footnote 1 says more realistic marketing models reduce to the model here, citing [3]; this reduction is not argued in the text (lines 40-41).
The first-mover analysis is restricted to a duopoly with two players and to disjoint or directed line structures (Section 4).
No empirical evaluation, no real network data, and no computational experiments are reported.

summary_md:
Bharathi, Kempe and Salek extend the independent cascade model so that several players compete. Each player seeds a set of nodes. Every node adopts the first colour that reaches it, activation delays are exponentially distributed, and simultaneous arrivals are broken at random. The paper proves four things. (1) If the opponent's seeds are fixed, a player's expected reach is monotone and submodular in its own seeds, so greedy seeding achieves (1-1/e) of the best response. This holds only for the last player to commit. (2) Uncoordinated equilibria lose at most a factor of 2 against a single controller of all seeds (the price of competition). (3) Pure Nash equilibria need not exist, and the first-mover problem is solved only on disjoint lines. (4) An FPTAS exists for single-player influence maximization on bidirected trees. The paper is purely theoretical: it uses no data, estimates no parameters, and reports no experiments.

The paper matters because Melange explicitly names it as the basis of its A/B coalition cascade (scenario.py:6-12). The CU colour is A and the anti colour is B, where B is the anti-tier members plus neutrals mobilized by industry money with probability min(0.9, $/400k). The system cites the paper's last-mover submodularity result to justify lazy greedy and its non-additivity reporting.

Reading the code turned up three departures. None of these points has been reproduced by a second path, so all are UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
- **Tie-breaking:** the cascade advances in synchronous hops and always processes A nodes first, so pro-CU wins every same-hop tie. The paper uses continuous random delays with random tie-breaking.
- **Frontier greedy:** the budget frontier ranks seeds by marginal spread times a leverage or competitiveness factor, not by raw marginal spread, so the clean (1-1/e) guarantee on spread does not apply. Electoral mode also removes opponent seeds, which Lemma 1 does not cover.
- **Coalition allocator:** it water-fills money in proportion to single-seed marginals and runs no greedy at all.

The paper also leaves an open question for the system: industry is modelled as a fixed opponent that never responds to CU's choices. The paper shows that once the rival best-responds, guarantees exist only for lines.

bearings.paper_claim: Independent cascade extended to two colours. Each edge gets its activation coin and an exponential delay fixed before the run. Lemma 1 builds a deterministic equivalent in which each edge outcome is fixed in advance and a node takes the colour of the path that reaches it. The paper's random tie-breaking applies only when several players select the same seed node, not to simultaneous arrivals.

bearings.system_side: Edge draws are keyed by iteration, u and v with no colour in the key, so one draw per edge serves whichever colour reaches it, and a coloured node is never recoloured. This matches the fixed-in-advance edge equivalence. The code drops the exponential delays and runs hop-synchronous spread. B is anti-tier members plus neutral bystanders drawn with probability min(0.9, industry dollars/400000); the code matches this.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Edge-level CRN and first-colour-wins carry over. Timing does not: unit hops replace the paper's continuous delays, so the paper's equivalence does not cover the system's timing. The bystander mapping (0.9 cap, 400000 scale) and the kernel constant 6 have no basis in the paper.

The paper uses continuous delays to avoid arrival ties and randomizes only between players who pick the same seed. The code structure matches the paper's edge equivalence; the hop timing is a departure.

gaps_exposed: No opponent response: industry is an exogenous bystander-mobilization rate, never a strategic seeder. Under the paper's results, CU's greedy plan is a best response only if industry has already committed and will not react. The system has no first-mover or equilibrium analysis and no sensitivity test of a reacting rival.

The tie-break is hop-synchronous with A processed first, not random, so pro-CU wins every same-hop contest. The size of this bias is unmeasured. A CRN rerun with randomized or B-first frontier order would bound it.

The cascade has no timing model. The paper's exponential delays make arrival order depend on path timing, while the system uses unit hops. That affects who wins contested neutrals and cannot be calibrated, because the system has no join-timing data.

The (1-1/e) claim in scenario.py's docstring is broader than what the code satisfies. It holds only for coalition-mode frontier greedy with fac=1. It does not hold for leverage-weighted ranking, for contest plays that remove opponent seeds, or for the proportional water-fill coalition allocator.

The paper gives no empirical calibration: no edge probabilities, no saturation constant, and no money-to-seed mapping. The bystander rule min(0.9, $/400k) and the kernel constant 6 have no source in it.

Expected spread is a heuristic model output. It is not a probability that members will join or a measure of access (D-025), and the paper has no legislative data to calibrate it.

The competitiveness multiplier enters the frontier's greedy ranking through fac. Its premise that dollars buy more in competitive seats is not validated (D-104..D-108), and the paper does not support it.
The paper proposes neither of the two rejected SNA changes (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization). It does not use LDA as an edge source.
paul_alignment: The paper partly agrees with Paul's takeaway. He wants rival industries modelled explicitly (his margin note on Kim et al. 2025 about conflicting industries) and cheap scenario simulation (Fink). The paper gives the formal basis for treating rival industries as a competing colour, and the built Monte Carlo with common random numbers is a faithful live-edge implementation of the model. But Paul's notes treat competitive influence maximization as solved by greedy. The paper says greedy works only when the rival has already moved and will not react. If the rival responds, no pure equilibrium is guaranteed, and the first-mover problem is solved only on lines. Paul's position on this component should therefore record two caveats: industry is never strategic in the build, and the cascade breaks every tie in CU's favour. His Chen 2023 note that high-ranking pressure is 'not diminishing' challenges submodularity under linear-threshold contagion. It does not undercut the independent cascade result here, which is the regime Lemma 1 covers.

extraction.venue: Proceedings of the 13th Conference of the European Chapter of the ACL (EACL 2012), Avignon, France, pp. 10-17. Metadata hint confirmed.
extraction.document_type: Conference paper (short research paper, pp. 10-17 incl. references)
extraction.coverage: Full text read: all of _text/a8112dd8d508.txt (pp. 10-17), including Tables 1-4, figure captions and the full reference list. Figures 1-7 have no data in the text layer, so only their captions are used. Paul's markup: none. The brief lists no markup files, and no file matching this paper ID appeared in the _annots or annotations folders.
extraction.research_question: Do users with the same emotional-stability trait (Big Five; neurotic vs secure/calm) interact differently on Twitter? The paper examines homophily in who talks to whom, posting and retweeting rates, and the shape of the resulting networks (Sec. 1, pp. 10-11; Sec. 4, pp. 14-16).
extraction.theory: Big Five model (Norman 1963; Goldberg 1992). Offline evidence that secure people have more interaction partners (Kanfer and Tanaka 1993) and that socially anxious youths have fewer friends and choose anxious friends (Van Zalk et al. 2011), which the authors say they test online (Sec. 2.1, p. 11). No formal hypotheses are stated beyond expected trait homophily and structural differences.
extraction.data: Corpus "Personalitwit2" of about 200,000 posts (Sec. 3, p. 14). Sampled from the Twitter public timeline on 25-28 Dec 2011, plus each sampled user's page (up to 20 recent tweets), so most posts predate the window (p. 13). Retweets excluded. Over 13,000 users and about 7,800 ego-networks in total (public user as centre, related users as edges). English-only subset: 5,392 ego-networks (p. 14). Validation: Personage dataset, 8 balanced users x 20 sentences (Sec. 2.4, p. 12); 18 users (10 neurotic, 8 secure) checked against Analyzewords scores (Sec. 2.4, p. 13). Unit of analysis: post for scoring, user for the personality label (users with one post discarded), ego-network for the structure analysis.
extraction.method: Unsupervised personality tagger (Sec. 2.3, pp. 11-13). It uses Pearson correlations from Mairesse et al. 2007 (linguistic cues: exclamation/question marks, emoticons, numbers, long words, word repetition) and Quercia et al. 2011 (following, followers, retweets) in Table 2. A 2,000-post random sample sets the feature averages. Each post yields a secure (s), neurotic (n) or balanced (o) model; the user label is the modal model. Descriptive statistics on the ego-networks, the trait-homophily frequency count (Fig. 4), a posting/retweet/reply comparison (Fig. 5), and Gephi network analysis of neurotic vs calm subgraphs with path length and diameter (Figs. 6-7, p. 15). No inferential tests are reported.
extraction.identification: None. The design is descriptive and correlational. The authors do not address endogeneity, confounding or selection, and their own sampling is described as producing many scattered small networks (p. 15).

summary_md:
Celli and Rossi (EACL 2012) built an unsupervised tagger that labels Twitter users as neurotic, secure or balanced. It borrows published correlations: linguistic cues from Mairesse et al. 2007 (punctuation, emoticons, long words) and follower/following/retweet counts from Quercia et al. 2011. The tagger ran on about 200,000 English posts sampled from the public timeline in December 2011, giving 5,392 ego-networks. Validation is very small:
- 0.625 accuracy against a 0.5 baseline on 8 Personage users.
- Average F1 0.578 against Analyzewords on 18 users. Analyzewords is a LIWC-style proxy that does not measure the Big Five.

The descriptive results:
- Users tend to talk with others who share their trait. Fig. 4 gives no coefficient and no test.
- Neurotic users post and retweet more. Calm users reply slightly more.
- Neurotic subgraphs have longer chains: average path length 1.551 vs 1.334, diameter 6 vs 5. Calm subgraphs have more mutual ties.

There are no inferential tests and no identification strategy.

For Paul's systems this is a weak, era-bound source. Its main use is as a lineage and caution marker for the psychometrics stack:
- big5_traits.py uses the same Mairesse-style closed-vocabulary ES/N weights.
- The affective-N slot is anchored for convergence to LIWC, and Celli's validation has the same method-shared circularity: a LIWC-family tagger scored against a LIWC-family proxy.
- The trait-homophily claim is the only finding that touches a system decision. The system already tested persona homophily on its own corpus and found it UNEARNED (|r| <= 0.015). An uncoefficiented 2011 Twitter frequency count cannot overturn that.

Nothing here bears on susceptibility to pressure, which is what the receptivity layer's N slot assumes. Every bearing below is UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: An unsupervised ES tagger built from Mairesse et al. 2007 linguistic correlations (Table 2) scores 0.625 accuracy against a 0.5 majority baseline on Personage (8 users x 20 sentences). The authors call this in line with the state of the art. Prior text classifiers reached E.Stab. accuracy of 0.531-0.705 (Table 1).
bearings.system_side: big5_traits.py scores ES from closed-vocabulary category rates using Mairesse-lineage weights (ES: anx -.30, negemo -.25, i -.20, negate -.15, posemo +.10) and sets N = -ES. The system's held-out CV against RKH for ES is .258, one of its weakest traits.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Shared lineage only: both apply published Mairesse correlates to new text without local supervision. Celli's evidence covers 2011 English tweets from public users and 8 human-rated users. Congressional floor speech and interviews are a different genre and population. The paper does not show that the ES weights transfer, and its accuracy is barely above chance at that sample size. Use it as a historical benchmark for how weak unsupervised ES reading is, never as validation.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-psychometrics#Lexical Big Five (Ramey-style closed vocabulary)|Lexical Big Five (Ramey-style closed vocabulary)]]

bearings.paper_claim: Validation against Analyzewords (a LIWC-based proxy, worried = neurotic, upbeat = secure) on 18 users: neurotic P 0.8 / R 0.615 / F1 0.695; secure F1 0.462; average F1 0.578. The authors concede the proxy does not measure the Big Five and that upbeat does not equal secure.
bearings.system_side: affective_n is built from E-residualized, party-controlled LLM affective facets (pessimism, anxiety, depression, volatility). LIWC (i + negemo - posemo) is kept as the independent convergent-validity anchor (r = +.24, gate G3). No gold N criterion exists.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Celli's validation is circular: a LIWC-family feature set scored against a LIWC-family proxy, so agreement partly reflects shared method. The system's LIWC anchor is the same kind of convergence. The paper therefore reinforces the system's own caveat (gate tests construct integrity, not validity) and adds no criterion evidence. It does not carry over as support for N validity.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-psychometrics#Affective neuroticism slot and N genre-transfer tests|Affective neuroticism slot and N genre-transfer tests]]

bearings.paper_claim: Neurotic users post and retweet more, and calm users reply slightly more (Fig. 5, no values in the text). Neurotic networks form longer chains (average path 1.551 vs 1.334; diameter 6 vs 5), and calm networks have more mutual ties.
bearings.system_side: The receptivity layer puts affective N into susceptibility with a +.30 weight, on the Byrne premise that N degrades decisions under pressure: susc = .40 coop + .30 N - .20 dil - .10 dom. This feeds susc_mult and edge_mult on the cascade. The brain records that no N susceptibility signal has been demonstrated.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Celli measures communication style and ego-network shape, not response to pressure or persuasion. The data are anonymous 2011 public Twitter users with tagger-inferred labels, not legislators. The result gives no support for N as a susceptibility multiplier. The only thing that transfers is a caution: if text-N tracks posting volume, a volume confound could enter N. The system residualizes on E and party but has no stated volume control. That control is untested here.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-influence-engine#Receptivity layer (susceptibility, incentive, prospect domain, seed probability)|Receptivity layer (susceptibility, incentive, prospect domain, seed probability)]]

bearings.paper_claim: Users tend to converse with others who share their emotional-stability trait (trait homophily). This is reported as a frequency pattern in Fig. 4, with no coefficient and no test.
bearings.system_side: Persona homophily was tested on the settled corpus and found UNEARNED (|r| <= 0.015 against an earning bar of |r| >= 0.05). Persona-homophily edge weighting in cosponsor_route.py stays OFF.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The trait differs (ES vs agency/communion), and so does the population (2011 Twitter users vs members of Congress). The relation (@-conversation) differs from cosponsorship, and Celli gives no inferential test. The system's measured null on its own data outranks this. Do not cite Celli as grounds to reopen homophily routing.

gaps_exposed: No volume control is documented for the text-derived N slot. Celli finds neurotic-tagged users post and retweet more, so a text N built from rates could still co-vary with output volume. affective_n is residualized on E and party only (emit_affective_n.py), and this is untested.

The psychometrics stack still has no non-LIWC, non-LLM criterion for N/ES. Celli's validation shows the same circularity (a LIWC-family tagger scored against a LIWC-family proxy), so it does not help close the gap.
The system does not measure network shape by trait (path length, mutual-tie share) on member interaction layers. Even if it did, it would be descriptive only and should not become an influence claim.
flags: The homophily claim (Fig. 4) has no coefficients and no inferential test. Do not use it to argue for persona- or trait-homophily routing, which the system measured as UNEARNED (|r| <= 0.015).

Validation is tiny (8 Personage users and 18 Analyzewords users). Any citation of this paper's ES accuracy as support for big5_traits ES/N must carry the sample size and the note that the proxy does not measure the Big Five.
The paper does not argue for dropping regular cosponsorship edges or for per-edge volume normalization, so neither rejected SNA proposal is implicated.
Path-length and diameter differences describe Twitter conversation structure. They are not closeness, access or introduction measures (D-025) and must not be carried over as influence language.
paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this paper. It sits in the lineage he already treats as dated: unsupervised correlational trait reading in the Mairesse/LIWC tradition, older than Ramey, which he calls 'dated but foundational'. It is consistent with his reading of Birkenmaier, whose highlights criticize SVM-era, unvalidated text personality measures. For the receptivity layer, Paul wants traits to act as edge parameters on the response to pressure (Oropeza). Celli does not speak to pressure response at all: it is descriptive network shape for anonymous Twitter users. His note that the system's validity record undercuts trait-driven receptivity still stands, and this paper does not change it. His notes predate the persona-homophily null, and Celli's homophily anecdote should not revive that idea.

related.why: Same first author's later review of personality computing. It places this 2012 unsupervised tagger within the field's later threats and validity critiques.
Closed-vocabulary Big Five from text with ES reported and N = -ES, the template big5_traits.py follows. Ramey applies it to legislators, Celli to Twitter users.
Meta-analysis of LIWC-Big Five correlations. It gives the effect-size ceiling for the Mairesse-style cues Celli relies on.
Meta-analysis of predicting the Big Five from social media footprints. It benchmarks how weak Celli's 0.625 accuracy and 0.578 F1 are.
Offline Big Five friendship-network selection study. It is a stronger, longitudinal test of the trait homophily that Celli only describes.
Source of the N-under-pressure premise the receptivity layer uses. Celli's N findings concern conversation structure, not pressure response, so the two do not corroborate each other.
LIWC word-category foundations (negemo, first-person singular) behind both Celli's cues and the system's affective-N anchor.
Big Five prediction from Twitter text. It is the regression-based counterpart to Celli's unsupervised Twitter tagger.

meta.title: Getting Personal: A Deep Learning Artifact for Text-Based Measurement of Personality
meta.venue: Information Systems Research, 34(1):194-222 (March 2023; published online 28 March 2022)

extraction.title: Getting Personal: A Deep Learning Artifact for Text-Based Measurement of Personality
extraction.venue: Information Systems Research, 34(1):194-222 (March 2023; published online 28 March 2022)
extraction.document_type: Journal article; design science artifact paper with design evaluation and two forecasting case studies
extraction.coverage: Full text read: all lines 1-4297 of C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_text\71f46d6078b0.txt, pp. 194-222 including references. Online Appendices A-I are cited throughout (e.g., Appendix B user-level results, Appendix H COVID-19 case) but are not included in the text file, so those results are not covered. No Paul markup files were specified for this extraction, so paul_markup is empty.
extraction.research_question: RQ1: Relative to existing NLP methods, how effectively can DeepPerson detect personality dimensions from user-generated text? RQ2: Can enhanced personality measurement significantly improve downstream forecasting outcomes? (p. 195)
extraction.theory: Systemic functional linguistic theory (SFLT; Halliday and Hasan 2004) as kernel theory, with ideational, interpersonal and textual meta-functions mapped to design components (Table 2, p. 201). Big Five (five-factor model; Goldberg 1990) as the personality construct. Psycholinguistic link between psychological states and language (Pennebaker and King 1999). For the downstream case, upper echelons theory (Hambrick 2007) is cited for links between executive traits and firm outcomes. Prediction is framed per Shmueli and Koppius (2011), not causal explanation (p. 196).
extraction.data: Design evaluation (Section 4): (1) PANDORA (Reddit), 3,000,566 comments from 1,568 users per the text (Table 3 lists 3,000,068 posts); (2) myPersonality (Facebook), 10,000 status updates from 250 users per the text (Table 3 lists 9,917); (3) Essays, 2,479 essays from 2,479 psychology students (1.9 million words). Labels are survey-based Big Five, median-split to binary per dimension. Splits are 50/25/25 at the user level, repeated 10 times. Pretraining/pseudo-labeling corpora: 1B Word benchmark and Sentiment140 (Go et al. 2009). Downstream case (Section 5): 352 senior executives (219 CEOs, 40 CFOs, 22 CXOs, 188 directors, 62 presidents, 10 chairmen per text; these sum to 541, not reconciled in text) at S&P 1500 firms (425 firms identified), employed 1990-2017 with Twitter accounts; tweets 2006-2017, mean 529 per executive (~186,000 data points); Compustat financials 1990-2017; 519 firm-executive-biennial observations; dependent-variable N ranges 405-519 (Table 10). Unit: user (design eval); firm-executive-two-year period (case study).
extraction.method: DeepPerson artifact has three parts: (a) CNN-LSTM encoder: CNN character encoder, word CNN embeddings, two multilayer Bi-LSTMs (ELMo-style, pretrained on 1B Word), one for syntax/semantics and one for LIWC/MRC/SPLICE psychological concept embeddings, aggregated to 1,024-dim (Eqs. 1-3, pp. 200-202); (b) wlpHAN, word-layer-person hierarchical attention with layer attention (Eq. 4), word attention (Eq. 6), and a person-level Bi-LSTM (Eq. 7), softmax over Big Five categories (Eqs. 8-9, pp. 202-204); (c) SPDFiT, self-taught fine-tuning: Bayesian pseudo-labeling with Gaussian class-conditional priors, entropy-based quality score s_m in [0,1] that both filters and scales SGD learning rate (Algorithm 1, p. 206; Section 3.3, pp. 204-206). Implemented on ELMo in PyTorch; mini-batch 500, dropout 0.5, grid search on validation users. Metrics: macro-averaged F, precision, recall, accuracy, AUC; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Downstream: Big Five scores as features added to baseline features in random forest regression (RFR) and gradient boosted decision trees (GBDT), scikit-learn, 20 estimators; comparators CNN-1, CNN-2, BERT, PersonaBERT, and ARIMA; outcomes measured as the log of the first two-year average after executive entry; improvement = (MSE_baseline - MSE_experimental)/MSE_baseline; Wilcoxon tests (p. 215-216).
extraction.identification: None in a causal sense. The authors explicitly frame the downstream test as prediction, not explanation (p. 196, citing Shmueli and Koppius 2011), and acknowledge reverse causality concerns (Hambrick 2007) without resolving them (p. 196). Identification of value is incremental predictive lift: the same RFR/GBDT models are run with and without personality features, with a chronological train/test structure referenced for the main case and a single chronological split reported in Online Appendix G (p. 217). Personality is assumed stable over the analysis period (p. 214, citing Cobb-Clark and Schurer 2012).
extraction.scope: Population: social media and essay authors (Reddit, Facebook, psychology students) for detection; S&P 1500 senior executives of US-listed firms for finance forecasting (Section 5). Era: Essays and myPersonality/PANDORA social media data; executive tweets 2006-2017; firm financials 1990-2017; paper published 2022. Institutional setting: IS design science; no institution-level or legislative/lobbying/electoral population is studied in the body text. The COVID-19 case (state and world leaders, Online Appendix H) is referenced but not in the text file. Languages: English implied; not explicitly stated. Nothing in the text addresses lobbying, networks, path-finding, allocation, elections, persuasion, turnout, or legislators, except that Hambrick (2007) is cited for personality being relevant to whether people are elected into leadership roles (p. 196).

key_findings.finding: On PANDORA, DeepPerson reaches AUC 75.0 vs. best comparators AttRCNN 64.6, CNN-1 64.0, PersonaBERT 63.4; macro F 65.1 vs AttRCNN 59.5. Text says DeepPerson beats best comparators by 5-15 pp across measures.
key_findings.numbers: AUC 75.0; Imp. +33.7% vs IBM baseline; AttRCNN AUC 64.6 (+15.2%)

key_findings.finding: On myPersonality, DeepPerson reaches AUC 70.7 vs AttRCNN 63.3 and PersonaBERT 61.2; macro F 67.0 vs 59.0 for AttRCNN. Wilcoxon tests significant (p<0.01) vs CNN-1 on most traits.

SPDFiT is the largest single contributor. Removing wlpHAN drops AUC by about 5 pp. Replacing SPDFiT with UDA, Self-Ensembling, logistic/Lasso/Ridge pseudo-labeling, or BERT variants lowers AUC from 70.0 to 58.3-65.2. Ablation is on PANDORA.
key_findings.numbers: CNN-LSTM (SPDFiT) AUC 70.0 (+20.1%); 1BWord only 62.3; UDA 65.1; Self-Ensembling 65.2; Logistic 64.9; BERT-Base 60.2; PersonaBERT 63.4; Doc2Vec 58.3

key_findings.finding: SPDFiT still beats comparators when only part of the unlabeled data is used: about 50% of unlabeled data gives fairly good results, and SPDFiT outperforms all alternatives at 40%+ of PANDORA or 30%+ of myPersonality unlabeled data.
key_findings.numbers: Unlabeled proportion tested in 10% steps from 10% to 100%

key_findings.finding: wlpHAN outperforms other attention networks. Full wlpHAN AUC 70.3 vs AttRCNN 64.6, HCAN 61.1, HAN 60.7, Msg-Attn 60.5; text reports 3-6 pp lift over those networks and 5-11% relative gains (all p<0.01). Each of the syntax/semantic, concept, and person encoders adds about 2 pp (text claim).
key_findings.numbers: wlpHAN AUC 70.3 (+20.0%); SynSem+Concept+Word 68.0; SynSem+Word 66.2; Word only 64.0 (+9.2%); aspect attention DPA 64.7, CA 63.9, GA 64.8

key_findings.finding: Downstream: adding DeepPerson Big Five scores improves forecasts of firm policy and performance indicators. Average MSE improvement for GBDT is 14.29%, and for RFR 6.67%. Text reports 6.1-14.3% average range across models and MSE/MAE, and 4-15% per variable. Gains for all eight DVs are significant at p<0.05.
key_findings.numbers: GBDT MSE avg +14.29% (CH 20.91, SG&A 31.74, INVEST 11.91, LEVER 12.95, IC 8.65, D&E 8.13, ROA 12.52, CF 7.49); RFR MSE avg +6.67%; GBDT MAE avg +9.46%

key_findings.finding: Comparators add less or nothing downstream. GBDT average MSE improvement: CNN-1 3.38%, BERT 8.62%, CNN-2 -1.80%. ARIMA time-series model is worse, with about 17% higher MSE than GBDT-DeepPerson (ARIMA average -17.05%).
key_findings.numbers: CNN-1 GBDT avg 3.38; BERT GBDT avg 8.62; CNN-2 GBDT avg -1.80; ARIMA GBDT avg -17.05

key_findings.finding: Error analysis: on instances where DeepPerson most beats comparators, synsem and concept embeddings and SPDFiT yield the largest MSE gains across all five traits. key_findings.finding: Design evaluation uses user-level Pearson correlation and MSE to approximate user Big Five scores. Text says DeepPerson is at least 10-18 points higher in correlation and at least 10% lower MSE than the best comparator on PANDORA and myPersonality (user-level results in Online Appendix B, not in text file).

Predictors: lagged performance and policy indicators, log total assets, ROA, cash flow, SIC code, executive age, gender, income, education, reputation (count of Google news mentions), LIWC sentiment, LDA top-10 topics, tweet count, followers, favorites (pp. 214-215)
Personality stability assumed over the analysis window (p. 214)
limitations: Authors state: bias is an important consideration for NLP models (Lalor et al. 2022); future work on other languages and on audio and video inputs would be beneficial (p. 219).
Authors state the design evaluation covered only social media posts, forum messages, and essays; speech transcripts and written articles may warrant exploration (p. 219).

Authors acknowledge reverse causality concerns in personality-outcome research (Hambrick 2007) but argue they do not undermine the prediction value of personality measures (p. 196). No causal claims are made.
Authors assume personality is stable over the analysis window, citing Cobb-Clark and Schurer (2012) (p. 214).

Detection model is trained on myPersonality (Facebook) labels and applied to executives' tweets (p. 214). The text reports no validation of executive-level scores against survey measures; user-level validation covers PANDORA and myPersonality only (Appendix B).

Internal inconsistencies in the text: abstract says DeepPerson improves detection by 10-20 pp (p. 194), body says 5-15 pp vs best comparators (p. 209). Text says 3,000,566 Reddit comments and 10,000 Facebook status updates (pp. 205-206), Table 3 lists 3,000,068 posts and 9,917 updates. Executive job-title counts sum to 541 against 352 executives, unreconciled (p. 214).

Essays comparison sample is psychology students (2,479 essays), not executives or public actors.

summary_md: Yang, Lau and Abbasi (ISR 2023) build DeepPerson, a design-science artifact for Big Five detection from text. It stacks an ELMo-style CNN-LSTM encoder (one Bi-LSTM for syntax and semantics, one for LIWC/MRC/SPLICE concept embeddings), a word-layer-person hierarchical attention network (wlpHAN), and SPDFiT, a Bayesian pseudo-labeling fine-tuner whose entropy quality score both filters pseudo-labels and scales the learning rate. Labels are self-report Big Five median-split to binary. On PANDORA (Reddit, 1,568 users) DeepPerson reaches AUC 75.0 vs 64.6 for the best comparator (AttRCNN), 63.4 PersonaBERT, 61.5 BERT-Base, and roughly 56 for the IBM feature-based baseline; on myPersonality (Facebook, 250 users) AUC 70.7 vs 63.3. Essays-corpus results sit in an appendix not in the text file. Ablations credit SPDFiT most, wlpHAN about 5 pp, and the LIWC-type concept encoder about 2 pp. Downstream, adding DeepPerson scores to GBDT forecasts of eight Compustat outcomes for 352 S&P 1500 executives with Twitter accounts cuts MSE by 14.29% on average (RFR 6.67%); this is framed as prediction, not causation, and executive-level scores are never validated against surveys. For Melange the paper is a benchmark showing that closed-vocabulary linear scoring, which the lexical Big Five uses, is the weakest family on self-report criteria, while LIWC concepts still add signal inside a deep model. It does not touch legislators, elite speech genres, observer or gold-panel criteria, or lobbying responsiveness, so its accuracy numbers are UNSTRATIFIED by genre and population relative to the system, and nothing here is reproduced (UNVERIFIED per DE-062).

extraction.title: Complex Contagion Influence Maximization (RL4CCIM)
extraction.venue: IJCAI-23 (Proceedings of the Thirty-Second International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence), pp. 5531-5540. Metadata hint had blank venue, year and DOI; the venue and year are taken from the running header in the text.
extraction.document_type: Conference paper (IJCAI-23 proceedings, algorithmic/ML benchmark study)
extraction.coverage: Full extracted text read in all chunks (1,329 lines, about 57k chars): title, abstract, introduction, related work, problem formulation, RL4CCIM method, experiments, ablation, limitation, conclusion, references (printed pp. 5531-5540). Appendices A-E (proofs, hyperparameters, network descriptions, MIP formulation, India seed comparison) are cited in the text but are not in the extracted file, so they are not covered. Annotations: all 74 items read (67 Highlight, 6 Ink, 1 FreeText). Only the FreeText item carries note text; it is stored truncated mid-word ("as varia"). Page numbers below are PDF page indices as used in the annotation file (printed journal page = PDF page + 5530). Lobbying, elections, legislators, text measurement, and turnout/persuasion are not discussed in the text; the closest topics are social-network seeding, budget-constrained target selection, and social reinforcement in adoption.
extraction.research_question: Can reinforcement learning be used to solve complex contagion influence maximization (CCIM): choosing a fixed budget of seed nodes when cascade probability rises with the number of already-activated neighbors, so the objective is non-submodular? (Sec. 1, PDF p2)
extraction.theory: Influence cascades are modeled as independent cascade (IC) or linear threshold (LT), both submodular, so greedy seeding has guarantees (Kempe et al. 2003). Complex contagion (Centola and Macy 2007) makes adoption probability jump when enough neighbors are active (S-shaped diffusion, Backstrom et al. 2006), which breaks submodularity and creates complementarities among seeds. The K-complex model (Eq. 1) sets activation probability to p0 when at least K neighbors are active and p1 otherwise, with 0 <= p1 << p0 <= 1. The authors frame seed selection as an MDP where each time step adds one seed, and reward is the marginal spread gain; sparse rewards are the central obstacle.
extraction.data: Nine networks; no observation period is stated in the extracted text, and the study simulates cascades rather than using observed adoption data. Unit: network nodes (individuals in the social networks). Five small social networks collected from homeless youth shelters in Los Angeles: CHANGE, DC, DOSIM, MFP, SPY. Four public networks: Football (Girvan and Newman 2002), Polbooks (Rossi and Ahmed 2015), India (Banerjee et al. 2013), Exhibition (Isella et al. 2011). Node counts appear in the text only for India (202 nodes) and SPY (67 nodes); other sizes are in Appendix C, which is not in the extract. Basic setting: p0=1, p1=0 (deterministic), seed budget T=8 (T=12 for Exhibition), threshold K=3 for CHANGE-SPY, K=4 for Football, Polbooks, India, K=6 for Exhibition.
extraction.method: Algorithmic benchmark, no causal design. Proposed RL4CCIM builds on the RL4IM/S2V line (Khalil et al. 2017; Chen et al. 2021) and uses Double-DQN (Van Hasselt et al. 2016) with four changes: (1) Solution filtering: candidate set A is the union of neighborhoods of every node with at least K neighbors; exploration samples from A with probability eps*eps', eps' annealed from 0.99 to 0 (Alg. 1 lines 3-5, 9; Thm 3). (2) Reward-based prioritized experience replay with priority (|delta| + beta*r + eps)^alpha (Eq. 5). (3) Reward shaping r' = r + omega*r_global, where r_global is the action's marginal contribution given all seeds chosen in the episode (Eqs. 6-7); this needs a full simulation before per-step rewards are assigned. (4) Graph attention network (GAT) replaces S2V as the graph encoder. Baselines: Random+ (seeds drawn from A, 50 runs averaged), Greedy (Kempe et al. 2003), DPIM (Angell and Schoenebeck 2017; authors' own reimplementation because code is not public), RL4IM (Chen et al. 2021), and OPT from a Gurobi mixed-integer program on small networks only (12-hour limit, exceeded from SPY onward per text). RL methods: 15 runs, best model chosen by validation every 20 training steps. Training finishes within 2 hours. Hyperparameters are in Appendix B (not in extract).
extraction.scope: Algorithmic influence maximization on nine small to medium social and contact networks, with simulated K-complex cascades. Population: no human subjects; the five shelter networks come from LA homeless youth shelters, cited to Wilder et al. 2021 for the HIV-prevention setting. Institutions: a multi-institution computer science and AI group (William and Mary, CMU, NTU, USC, Harvard). Era: IJCAI-23, 2023. The paper says training time and scalability are not the focus, so all experiments use small networks. Nothing here addresses lobbying, elections, legislators, text measurement, or turnout.

key_findings.finding: Complex contagion influence maximization is non-submodular (Theorem 1) and K-complex contagion IM is NP-hard (Theorem 2), shown by reduction from IC when K=1. Proofs are in Appendix A, which is not in the extract.
key_findings.numbers: None reported beyond the K=1 reduction

key_findings.finding: Reward sparseness has two sources: effective-solution sparseness (few seed sets activate anyone) and credit sparseness (rewards stay flat until several seeds are chosen).
key_findings.location: Sec. 1 PDF p2; Sec. 5.1 PDF p4 (printed 5534)
key_findings.numbers: Toy network (Fig. 2, 8 nodes, p0=1, p1=0, K=3, T=4): 17 of C(8,4)=70 four-seed sets are effective, 24.3%. Seed sequence {1,2,3,5} gives per-step rewards 1,1,1,2.

key_findings.finding: Solution filtering keeps only nodes that could be part of an effective solution (neighborhoods of nodes with at least K neighbors). Theorem 3 says no effective solution is excluded.
key_findings.numbers: Toy example: feasible sets shrink from 70 to 15, which is 21.4% of the original space. The text also says 24.2% of nodes (not sets) have non-zero reward, which conflicts with 24.3% in Sec. 5.1.

key_findings.finding: In the deterministic basic setting, RL4CCIM has the highest normalized influence on all nine networks, by the authors' account, with some ties.
key_findings.numbers: Football 1.0 (RL4IM 0.513, DPIM 0.3913, Greedy 0.3217); Polbooks 0.819 (RL4IM 0.7429, DPIM 0.6762); India 0.5347 (DPIM 0.3911, RL4IM 0.3465, Greedy 0.0396); Exhibition 0.5585 (DPIM 0.5537, RL4IM 0.5439, Greedy 0.0293); CHANGE 0.283, tied with DPIM and RL4IM (Greedy 0.1509).

key_findings.finding: On small networks where exact MIP gives a value, RL4CCIM matches the optimum on DC and DOSIM and is slightly below it elsewhere.
key_findings.numbers: DC 0.4634 = OPT; DOSIM 0.375 = OPT; CHANGE 0.283 vs OPT 0.3019 (about 6.3% below, derived); MFP 0.3472 vs 0.375 (about 7.4% below, derived); SPY 0.5075 vs 0.5522 (about 8.1% below, derived).

key_findings.finding: Greedy performs very poorly on some networks. The authors say it finds no effective solution on India (202 nodes).
key_findings.location: Sec. 6.1 PDF p7; seed comparison in Appendix E (not in extract)
key_findings.numbers: Greedy 0.0396 on India vs RL4CCIM 0.5347; Random+ 0.0498 on India; Greedy and Random+ both 0.0293 on Exhibition.

key_findings.finding: RL4IM and DPIM are unstable across networks. The authors attribute DPIM's gaps to its hierarchy assumption and RL4IM's to effective-solution sparseness that grows with solution-space size. Both explanations are stated as hypotheses.
key_findings.numbers: RL4IM Football 0.513 vs 1.0; DPIM Football 0.3913 and India 0.3911 vs RL4CCIM 1.0 and 0.5347.

key_findings.finding: RL4CCIM beats all baselines across a sensitivity sweep of propagation probability, budget and threshold on India, Football and Polbooks. Greedy jumps on India when T rises from 12 to 14 and K falls from 4 to 3, which the authors attribute to a larger share of effective solutions.
key_findings.numbers: p1 in {0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1}; T in {6, 8, 10, 12, 14}; K in {2, 3, 4, 5, 6} (K=5 used for Football T-sweep). Fig. 4 plotted values are not in the extracted text.

key_findings.finding: Ablation on India: removing each component lowers normalized influence, and removing all of them (which equals RL4IM) lowers it most.
key_findings.numbers: Drops: w/o solution filtering 10.2%; w/o PER 4.6%; w/o reward shaping 9.3%; w/o GAT 21.3%; w/o all components 35.2%.

key_findings.finding: Scalability is the main limitation: simulation time for complex contagion is the top bottleneck, followed by Q-network gradient cost on large graphs. Pruning is suggested as a remedy.
key_findings.numbers: All experiments use small networks; RL training finishes within 2 hours (Sec. 6 PDF p6).

key_findings.finding: Solution filtering alone and PER alone each contribute a measurable share of the gain, and the authors judge the combined components necessary.
key_findings.numbers: See ablation drops above (10.2% and 4.6% respectively).

limitations: Scalability: complex-contagion simulation cost and Q-network training cost limit the method to small networks; the authors present pruning as an unexplored fix (PDF p8).
The paper says training time and scalability are not its focus; all experiments run on small networks (PDF p6).

The DPIM baseline is the authors' own reimplementation (original code not public), using a Jaccard-similarity hierarchical decomposition (PDF p6). Results for this baseline therefore depend on that implementation.

The MIP optimum was reported as exceeding the 12-hour limit starting at SPY (67 nodes), yet Table 1 gives an OPT value for SPY (0.5522). This conflict is not explained in the text and should be checked.
Table 1 is limited to the deterministic setting (p1=0, p0=1). Stochastic propagation appears only in Fig. 4, and its plotted values are not in the extracted text.
K and T were chosen by the authors per network to keep spread neither too sparse nor too dense (PDF p7), so the reported comparisons depend on those choices.
Only nine networks are tested, and the paper does not test transfer to new networks, which it lists as future work (Conclusion, PDF p8).

Node heterogeneity is absent: Eq. 1 applies one threshold K and one pair (p0, p1) to every node, with no node-level status or rank term. Paul's margin note asks about high-ranking members, and the text does not address that question.

Internal inconsistencies: the 24.3% vs 24.2% figure for effective solutions (Sec. 5.1 vs 5.3, where 24.2% is described as a share of nodes, not solutions); and the ablation text says 'removing the 3 components altogether' while listing four components and an all-removed variant (Sec. 6.3).
The definition of 'normalized influence' used as the outcome in Table 1 and Figs. 4-5 is not given in the extracted text.
The explanations for DPIM and RL4IM instability are the authors' hypotheses and were not tested in the paper (PDF p7).
Appendices A-E (proofs, hyperparameter ranges, network descriptions, MIP formulation, seed comparison) were not in the extract, so claims that depend on them cannot be checked here.
The paper tests simulated cascades only; it does not validate the K-complex model against field adoption data, though it cites Centola 2010 and Romero et al. 2011 as empirical support.

summary_md: Chen, Wilder, Qiu, An, Rice and Tambe (IJCAI-23) study seed selection when adoption follows complex contagion: under their K-complex model a node activates with probability p0 once at least K neighbours are active and p1 otherwise. They prove the objective is non-submodular and NP-hard, then frame seeding as an MDP solved by Double-DQN (RL4CCIM). Four additions address sparse rewards: solution filtering to nodes near a degree-K hub, reward-prioritised replay, a global marginal-contribution reward and a GAT encoder. On nine small networks with deterministic cascades (p0=1, p1=0, budget T=8 or 12), RL4CCIM has the best normalised influence everywhere, sometimes tied. Greedy collapses on India (0.0396 vs 0.5347). RL4CCIM matches the MIP optimum on DC and DOSIM and comes within about 6 to 8 percent elsewhere. In the India ablation, the drops are 10.2 to 35.2 percent. There are no field data: cascades are simulated, and scale is the stated limit. For Paul's system the paper does not supply an estimate. It is a warning about an assumption. The coalition engines (budget frontier, per-topic coalition, dashboard budget recruit) run a simple-contagion independent-cascade kernel and greedy or knee logic justified by diminishing returns. If real cosponsor joining is threshold-like, as the LT priming module already assumes one target at a time, those greedy paths can miss jointly valuable seed sets. They would also drop candidates whose solo marginal is zero. The useful takeaway is a test, not a method swap: measure whether CU-bill join hazards jump with the count of already-joined close partners. Until that is checked, read greedy guarantees as properties of the model kernel only. This bearing analysis is UNVERIFIED per DE-062.

bearings.paper_claim: Complex-contagion IM is non-submodular (Thm 1) and NP-hard (Thm 2). Greedy can be arbitrarily bad: normalised influence 0.0396 for Greedy vs 0.5347 for RL4CCIM on India (202 nodes), and 0.0293 vs 0.5585 on Exhibition. bearings.system_side: budget_frontier.py runs a lazy-greedy heap over a candidate pool with MAXSEEDS default 60 (line 7). Spread comes from an edge-keyed IC cascade over the P kernel (lines 83-94). The loop stops when the best marginal is zero (inside lines 161-172). The knee is the last seed whose gain is at least a quarter of the peak gain on the spread path (frontier_knee, lines 49-58, called at line 172). Both the stop rule and the knee presume diminishing returns.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The zero-marginal failure bites only if real cosponsor joining is threshold-like, so that single-seed marginals are zero until K partners are joined. Under the system's per-edge IC kernel the stop rule and knee are internally coherent. The paper's numbers are simulated cascades on non-legislative networks, so they do not transfer as estimates.
bearings.verifier_note: Table 1 values for Greedy and RL4CCIM on India and Exhibition match the claim. Setting, Thm 1 and Thm 2 match the text. Code claims about MAXSEEDS 60, the zero-marginal stop, the IC-style cascade and the quarter-peak knee were checked at the cited lines. The knee is an inclusive rule on gains, equivalent to 4 x gain at least peak.

summary_issues: Summary says nine small networks. The paper's nine are five small shelter networks (CHANGE, DC, DOSIM, MFP, SPY) and four larger public networks (Football, Polbooks, India, Exhibition); India alone has 202 nodes (Sec. 6.1, PDF p7).

Summary says four additions address sparse rewards. The paper ties only the first three (solution filtering, reward-prioritised replay, global reward shaping) to the two sparseness causes. The GAT encoder is a representation change (Sec. 5.2, PDF p4).

Summary says the India ablation drops are 10.2 to 35.2 percent. Single-component drops are 4.6 (wo-PER), 9.3 (wo-RS), 10.2 (wo-SF) and 21.3 (wo-GAT) percent. Removing all components gives 35.2 percent (Sec. 6.3, PDF p7).

Summary says all coalition engines run an IC cascade with greedy or knee logic. The dashboard budget-recruit uses one-hop coverage probabilities, not a cascade. Per-topic coalition is a one-pass marginal ranking with water-fill, not greedy.

Summary and table use the SPY OPT value 0.5522 as a MIP optimum. The paper says the MIP exceeded its 12-hour limit from SPY onward, so the SPY OPT figure is unverified. The 6 to 8 percent gap claim is weaker for SPY than stated.
Gap item says greedy paths exist in per-topic coalition. That engine is not greedy (see bearing 2), so the gap wording should name only the budget frontier.
Bearing 2 said the top 45 candidates are ranked by solo marginal. The code ranks them by engagement score ev before computing marginals (per_topic_coalition.py line 114).
Bearing 2 paper_location cites Sec. 1 PDF p2 for the 17-of-70 and 24.3 percent figures. Those numbers appear only in Sec. 5.1 (PDF p4) and Sec. 5.3 (24.2 percent).
Coverage: the Thm 1 proof sits in Appendix A, which is absent from the extracted text. Thm 1 is verified only as a stated theorem, and Appendices B to E were not checked.
Paul note: the only annotation text is one FreeText item truncated mid-word; the paul_alignment reading is consistent with it but cannot be confirmed in full.
gaps_exposed: No test of simple vs complex contagion in cosponsorship: join hazard on CU bills as a function of the number of already-joined close partners (exposure curve) has not been measured.
Greedy paths in the budget frontier and per-topic coalition have no exact or exhaustive baseline on a small topic to bound their optimality gap if spread were non-submodular.
Candidates with zero solo marginal are dropped before allocation (per_topic_coalition.py:116); seeds valuable only in combination are invisible by construction.
The frontier knee is read as diminishing returns; a flat-then-jump curve, which threshold adoption produces, would be misread as an early knee or stop.
No source-status (leadership or rank) term in the cascade kernel, the gap Paul's margin note raises; the paper's homogeneous K does not fill it.
flags: No conflict with D-025, D-021 or the rejected SNA proposals: the paper argues for neither dropping regular cosponsorship edges nor per-edge volume normalisation, and uses no LDA data.
All bearings above are agent analysis and stay UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces them (DE-062).
Any count-dependent cascade variant must keep the two cpf physics separate (architecture rule); this paper does not justify merging them.

Paper-internal issues: SPY OPT 0.5522 is reported although the MIP is said to exceed 12 hours from SPY onward; 24.3 vs 24.2 percent effective-solution figures; ablation text says three components while listing four.
Paul's only note is truncated mid-word (as varia), so its full intent cannot be confirmed.
paul_alignment: Paul's entry has no takeaways or system links; his one margin note questions diminishing returns for high-ranking members and ties pressure susceptibility to some variable. That instinct agrees with the paper's central point that seed value need not diminish, though the paper models it through neighbour-count thresholds with homogeneous K, not node status. The note is not stale: the system as built still assumes diminishing returns in the budget frontier knee and coalition ranking, and its kernel has no leadership term.
